utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom. Mr. Ierace -- Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, to begin with, to everybody. I merely wanted to say that General Galic tells me that on his monitor the date of the hearing is incorrect, and on my monitor I simply have no dates. I don't know whether this is important and how important it is, but I merely wished to tell you about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It says the 13th of February on my screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not this date. The day of the hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it day 196 or -- it's not quite clear to me. Perhaps, General Galic, you could tell us what you see and what is not correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. I don't know whether it is important, as Mr. Piletta-Zanin, my lawyer, has said. But it says here the date -- it is the 169th day of the trial, and according to my record yesterday it was 193rd or 194th day. So obviously something has gone wrong here. My apologies if something is wrong, but I don't think I am, because I keep record.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The counsel's microphone is switched off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Piletta-Zanin, it is easier for interpreters when you switch on your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When I look at my list of transcripts, I see on the 12th of February day 195 and today 196. Therefore, it -- and it now says --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 169.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 169. One-six-nine, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It should be 196. Yes. Of course. Thank you, General Galic, so that at least avoids that under the same name different transcripts will be stored on your computers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Guskova.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We had some difficulties with our computers. I apologise, but as a consequence of my manipulations I closed -- yes, I think it's functioning again. Yes. Ms. Guskova, Judge Nieto-Navia has one or more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Do you recall that -- are you hearing? Is it okay?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you receive translation? No, of course -- yes. Is the -- because what I would expect, as a matter of fact, a Russian interpreter to sit next to you. But --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry. I will be listening to the Serbian interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, may I just ask where -- I know that we have three interpreters' booths in this courtroom. And usually if there is translation in a fourth language, the interpreter is sitting next to the witness in the seat. The chair is there. Is there Russian translation effective at this moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was about to ask you for the permission to listen to the Serbian interpretation and to answer in Russian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would the interpreters in B/C/S, would they be able to translate into English and into French if the witness speaks Russian? I see that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it then, Ms. Guskova, that you are mastering of the -- as we call it the Bosnian/Serbian/Croatian language is sufficient to understand it and -- yes. We'll then proceed, you listen to the B/C/S and you answer in Russian. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have only one request: I -- may I remind you that yesterday you promised to give me the floor for a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. If you -- after we've put questions to you, you will get your few words. Yes. Please -- please listen to the question of Judge Nieto-Navia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Do you recall that yesterday we saw the numbers of the 1991 census? Do you recall the ethnic groups shown in that census?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is nodding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: You're nodding. That means --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Yes? Do you recall the names of those groups?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ethnic groups. I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Could you please tell me. Tell me the names.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslims, Serbs, and Croats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: And Yugoslavs?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were also Yugoslavs. I'm referring to the three main groups.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: My question was the following: We know who are the Serbs, who are the Croats, and who are the Muslims. Do you know who are the Yugoslavs?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Yes. Tell me.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: After 1945, the Yugoslav society set out to create a new type of ethnicity, to be called Yugoslav. Just as the Soviet Union was of many different ethnic groups, ethnic communities, was doing the same. Once upon a time we were also on the way to create the Soviet people. The idea of a unification of South Slavic peoples was -- found its reflection in the new name for people who wanted to give proof -- to give manifestation of their internationalism. And therefore, in every republic at the time of population censuses, everybody could, rather than his natural ethnicity, his ethnicity by birth, also declare that he was a Yugoslav.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: The Yugoslavs -- the Yugoslav group was it composed then by Muslims, Serbs, and Croats?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are quite right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge El Mahdi has one or more questions for you. JUDGE EL MAHDI: Thank you, Mr. President. [Interpretation] Madam, I have to tell you that I read your report with great interest, and it therefore prompted me to start to seek for a large number of -- for further information. Therefore, I will ask you some questions which would mostly be meant to clarify certain points. I do not know whether you have the English translation before you of your report, which is titled "The position of Serbs." In English, it is on page 16. It comes after the subtitle "Arming of Muslims." Right? Therefore, the "The position of Serbs," towards the end of the last paragraph -- or rather, the one before the last, and I will quote it to you in English. [In English] "Representatives of the Serb population of Bosnia and Herzegovina addressed the Minister of Defence of Serbia, Mr. Simovic, with a request for help. Since all the military institutes were located in the territory where Muslims were a majority population, Minister of Defence proposed to Serbs, 'to plan actions for a forcible seizure of materiel and technical equipment from the warehouses,' to start training of fighters within the system of Territorial Defence, et cetera, and but in general to rely on their own forces." [Interpretation] Now, I'd like you to tell me why was this so and why did he turn to the Ministry of Defence of Serbia. That is one question. Secondly, do you know how did it happen and how did they lay their hands on the weapons from the military depots? Was it the Minister of Defence requisitioned those weapons from the depots? Were they under the control -- were these weapons under the control of the JNA? That is, I'd like you to tell us briefly a little bit more about this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have chosen a very interesting subject. One could really belabour the point at great length because it sheds much better light on the creation of forces in Bosnia and Herzegovina towards the end of 1991 and in the beginning of 1992. My first comment: Why did they turn to the Minister of Defence of Serbia? Because the Minister of Defence of Yugoslavia refused to talk with the Serbs from Bosnia and Herzegovina, to address that subject. And the Ministry of Defence of Serbia had just been -- had barely been established, had just been set up in 1991. And apart from the Minister of Defence and his cabinet, that ministry had no resources whatsoever, and they could not help any forces in other republics, of course apart from the moral support. And therefore, when they turned to the Ministry of Defence of Serbia, it offered a possibility to consult, to seek advice as to what to do if it's turned out that there was a shortage of needed weapons in case of the possible -- of the possible need for such weapons. And here I'd like to draw your attention to two dates. The Armed Forces of the republic of the Muslim side started their preparations in spring 1991, and the Serbs turned to the Ministry of Defence of Serbia only as late as autumn 1991, at the time when they could already sense the danger. And it is important that -- to say that the armed units did not have any such weapons. And therefore, the response of the Ministry of Defence tells us and proves to us that the preparations to set up armed units was still at the stage of consideration and search for possible solutions. And the minister was quite right that all -- that basically all of the military assets, all of the depots and plants, were in the Muslim territory, and that is why he suggested to share those weapons. And I'm aware of facts that that is what was done. That is, the Muslim side and the Serb side. And it depended on who headed a particular military formation or a depot or what particular ranks were close to those depots. If Muslims -- whether it was Muslims or Croats and Serbs, it depended on that, how the Serbs were then distributed in two or three sets, because at that time the Yugoslav People's Army had not yet disintegrated. That was only beginning. That is, that was the time when the officers started leaving following ethnic criteria, that is, depending on whether they were Muslims, Croats, or Serbs. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Right. So if I may, I'd like also to ask you: You said "representatives of the Serbs." Could you give us some names, the names of persons who were representatives?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean in the army? JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Well, yes -- no. What I mean is that in your report you say "representatives of the Serb population addressed the Ministry of Defence." Who was that? Who were those representatives? What -- whom did you mean by "Serb representatives"?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the Army of Republika Srpska did not exist yet, as no -- as no institution had come into being to reflect the Serbs, that was why those who represented Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina went. But I cannot give you the names, unfortunately, right now because I would need to have a look at the book, the book from which I took this information. And the book is practically a diary of the secretary of the Minister of Defence, Simovic. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] -- If I understand you correctly, you accepted this version as an accurate version. You accept this version. You go along with this version, don't you?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which one? JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] What you have put on paper. If I understand you correctly, you say -- you say you learnt about this fact from a diary. But do you then side along with this version? Did you verify it? Did you -- were you able to check whether it was true, whether that version was accurate? Right. You also say the minister advised them to act, and I quote, [In English] "to plan actions for a forcible seizure." [Interpretation] By force. Do you, therefore, also agree that what was said was what was later on carried out in practice?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are two different things, what the minister said and what all the three parties did later on when the Yugoslav People's Army fell apart. And how they acted? Well, they acted different. At times those were seizures by force, and there were also tricks, and there were also voluntary transfers. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you. I'd now like to broach another subject, if I may. I'm now referring to the heading [In English] "Serbs were making concessions". [Interpretation] It is page 26 in the English text, the third paragraph. Are you following me, madam? Very well. Then I quote. [In English] "Serb air force was completely blocked." [Interpretation] The paragraph which begins with the words [In English] "It was a question of the ban on military flights."

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is it where it begins with Dobrica Cosic and Franjo Tudjman? "Serbs were making concessions." Is that it? JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. French booth, I don't understand. Madam, it is a paragraph which begins with the words "it was a question of the ban," the third paragraph, on the page with the heading "Serbs were making concessions."

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't find it. Is it after the heading of Vance Owen -- Vance-Owen plan? JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Previous interpretation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the previous one. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Which previous -- "Serbs were making concessions." It is under this heading.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, right. But I can't find the paragraph. So could you tell me what is the preceding paragraph or the one after it. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] It is under that particular heading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I just try to assist. In the paragraph starting with "Serbs were making concessions." I think it's the third linear -- starting with, "It was a question of the ban on military flights." JUDGE EL MAHDI: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's approximately -- in the English version between line 10 and 15. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] It's more or less in the middle of the page, halfway down the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: It's after the footnote 164. After the footnote 164.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just to assist me a little bit, can you please specify. "Serbs were making concessions." This action starts with the words "Dobrica Cosic and --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then we have the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "The co-chairman of the international conference understood..." And then we have the third paragraph, which reads: "It was a question of the ban on military flights in the air space of Bosnia." And I think you're talking about the third -- JUDGE EL MAHDI: The third paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The third paragraph, consisting in English of three lines.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately I cannot find this paragraph. Maybe I will just try and answer your question. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] I'll quote to you in English. [In English] "Ban on military flights in the air space of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In this way Serb air force was completely blocked. In case of failure of the question would be raised in lifting the embargo on the supply," et cetera. [Interpretation] Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation] JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] So my question is, first of all: When you say "the Serb air force," you're referring to the air force of the Republic of Serbia or are you referring to something else? Is this the air force of the Republic of Serbia that was part of the new federation, the Yugoslav Federation, together with Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Security Council resolutions banned any flights over Bosnia-Herzegovina. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Yes. But not the air force. When you mention the air force, it's the military air force of the Republic of Serbia. And you say that you are aware of what Serbia did, that it was not to control the air space of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Have I understood this correctly?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I have a look at the English text, please. Yes. The Serb forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina were completely blocked. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Yes. But the air force, the prohibition -- you said here that military flights -- were you referring to the air force of the Republic of Serbia that was part of the old Yugoslav Federation, or did you mean that the forces present in Bosnia-Herzegovina had an air force at their disposal as well?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I believe I should have a look at the data, whether the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina had any aircraft at their disposal. I believe they did have some aircraft. That is why I would say that here. We're talking about the aircraft of the Republika Srpska. I have some data in the computer, and I have the data on who had how much weaponry. And if you're interested in precise data, I could quote you the exact number of aircraft and which party had how many of those. I believe that here we're talking about Republika Srpska. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] But I wanted to make sure that you wanted to say that this was a prohibition of flights with regard to aircraft that belonged to Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response] JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Yes. You are nodding. Yes. Well, thank you. So my last question is then -- I think I'm going to read this out. It's under the title "The essence of the conflict." It's page 11 and 12 in the English version, and it's the first four lines at the end of the first paragraph. I'll quote you in English: [In English] "He warned at the dangers of war." [Interpretation] If I've understood this correctly, you are referring to Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let us find this section. You're speaking about the assessment of the character of war. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Yes. But I would like to hear your interpretation. You say that Mr. Karadzic warns of the dangers of war. In your opinion, is this a threat? What context was this said? I'll finish the sentence. [In English] "if the leaders of Muslims and Croats should decide for a unilateral secession." [Interpretation] Did this express the desire not to accept anything and to go as far as war?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. I would like to first find this passage. I would like the interpreters to help me in which section would I find this paragraph. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] This title is called "The essence of the conflict in Bosnia." It's the first paragraph. It's at the very end, the last four lines, which start with the words [In English] "He warned of the dangers of war."

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Yes. My question is simply --

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It starts with the 24th of January in the version I have. I've found it. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] It says "Quoted in a television programme of the 2nd of November, 1991," where Mr. Karadzic said something to the effect of -- something like [In English] "He warned of the dangers of war." [Interpretation] In your opinion, was this a warning?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation] JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] He said that there would be war if there was no compliance. There were no means of negotiating. If the other side opted for independence, opted for secession from Yugoslavia, he said that in that case war would ensue. Is that how you understood this statement?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me for this delay. Since I failed to find this paragraph right on the spot. Here I have in mind that in November 1991 all the parties were ready to discuss together the issues of the threats for their republic. And after the events in Croatia, in Slovenia, the warnings of the threats of war or the dangers of war should have stopped the secession of Bosnia and Herzegovina from SFRY. This is how I would understand this statement by Karadzic. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] With the leave of Mr. President. You mentioned the two encirclements that Owen mentioned. [In English] "The first one was placed by Serbs shelling the city from artillery armament and sniper rifles and by placing a circle around the city. The second blockade was made by the army of the Bosnian government." [Interpretation] You remember this paragraph, don't you? In your opinion, is this information reliable? It's about history. When this is expressed as an academic in this domain, to what extent would you take these statements as truthful statements? Or would you have doubts about such statements? Do you as an academic, when Owen says or writes, would you say that his writings, his statements are a reliable source when carrying out scientific research? And in particular when he says -- I have to be quite clear. [In English] "The first one was placed --" [Interpretation] I'm quoting you. [In English] "The first one was placed by Serbs shelling the city with artillery, armament and sniper rifles and placing a circle around the city." [Interpretation] Do you accept these statements?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I shall answer both your questions, the first and the second question. Quoting Mr. Owen -- I was quoting Mr. Owen because I believe that if we don't have a historic distance from the events which we witnessed, then for us it is extremely important to consider all the diaries, memoir writings and especially for the crisis in the territory of the former Yugoslavia the appearance of such memoirs were extremely important from David Owen, Carl Bildt, MacKenzie, General Rose. That is why quoting from them would be quite justified from the academic point of view. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Yes, madam, I apologise, but my question is very simple. I'm asking you as an academic, as an expert. When you refer to Mr. Owen in your opinion, this is a reliable source, a reliable reference. That's all I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I absolutely agree with the issue about the double blockade. But with regard to formulation on this subject, I wouldn't concur. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. [In English] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. I've got a few question for you as well. But if you would first allow me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you a few questions. The first one is that in your report you write that those who reported as being Yugoslavs, you said these were mainly Serbs and children of mixed marriages. What is the source of this knowledge? You just answered to a question of Judge Nieto-Navia that they could have been of all ethnic origins, but in your report you described that the majority were Serbs or children from mixed marriages. Could you tell me what -- on the basis of what you have drawn that conclusion.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in order to see it precisely, I could have a look at the footnote in the text. But I would like to tell you that in statistics there is a special methodology for determining such cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whenever it is possible to compare the numbers of the previous, the subsequent censuses, then it becomes clear which numbers went up, which numbers went down, and which numbers stayed the same. This fact is not put to doubts in scientific literature that Muslims also ascribed themselves both from among Serbs, Croats, and would tell you that the numbers themselves were for the -- were testifying towards the Serbs, and we can also spread them out across the regions. Unfortunately, the census of 1991 was not considered as an official one. The last official census was the census of 1981. That is why the numbers, the exact numbers, could be determined only later. But talking about the historical aspect, as you have asked me, well, I can tell you that history as demonstrating to us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. As a matter of fact, I just asked you what was the source on which you have drawn this conclusion. You said you could look it up in the footnote. One of the reasons why I asked the question to you is because there is no footnote as far as I can see that would have enabled us to follow the sources. It's the --

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which number are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We are talking about the -- the first chapter reads "Causes of the Yugoslav crisis," and in the first subtitle is, "Causes of war in Bosnia-Herzegovina." And then it is the first -- the sixth paragraph starting with "Bosnia and Herzegovina was a centre republic of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia with a mixed population." And at the very end of this paragraph, you say that "5 and a half per cent decided at a given time to declare themselves as being Yugoslav and the majority among them was Serb or children from mixed marriages."

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see. I would like to refer you to footnote 117 and 91. The book which I'm referring to in footnote 91 is a book published by the Institute for Ethnology of the Russian Academy of Sciences where the issues of statistics were elaborated on in great detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And as far as statistics are concerned, if you tell us that it is by comparison to an earlier census that you could draw these conclusions, would a number of 5 and a half per cent where during ten years a huge number of new citizens would be part of the census? I mean, the population changes considerably over ten years. Would that allow for a conclusion such as you write it down? Is it your conclusion on the basis of this literature, or is this the conclusion of those that have written the articles or the books you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, undoubtedly. I was not involved myself in statistics matters, but I used the data of those experts who were working in that field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were you using the data or were you using the conclusions of those experts? Is it on the basis of their data that you've drawn your own conclusions or is it on the data that you've reflected those conclusions? Because what makes me this question to you is because you were very precise referring to pages very often but there's no footnote and no reference to whatever page in this specific paragraph.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps it is an error, but it can be easily corrected. I simply know what book it is. And in response to your question, I can say that I used both the data and the conclusions which the scientists included and presented in that book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that answer. You have drawn our attention to an intensive construction of new mosques. You compared the number of mosques and the newly constructed mosques. Could you tell us what exactly is the relevance of those data.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This information speaks about the atmosphere above all in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina until -- up to 1990s. No specialist and none of the citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina believed that Bosnia-Herzegovina could precisely be the place where inter-ethnic -- where the inter-ethnic strife or struggle, would start. And I suppose I was not a good specialist, because in the late 1980s I was saying that it could perhaps begin in Croatia, and I didn't believe that it would start in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But again, my question was -- and you partly answered it. You said it demonstrates the atmosphere. What atmosphere? You could interpret this in -- I would say in many different ways. I mean, you could interpret it as being that people became more -- Muslim people became more religious than they were before or that they -- well, a lot of possible interpretations of this fact. And I would like you to tell me what exactly you had in mind when you put this figure into your report as a relevant one for the conflict.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's have a look. Where did I write that down?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I haven't got the exact source. But you gave numbers. You said new mosques were constructed, and you compared with the number of the existing mosques. Yes?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did, yes. Yes. I've found it. Well, the purpose of it was to show the relations in the SFRY, that is, the central authorities and their attitude towards ethnic aspirations in other republics, and the attitudes in the republic itself and respect for the faith -- for the religions of all the three peoples which inhabited that republic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's still not quite clear to me. You say the purpose of it was to show the relations in the SFRY, that is, the central authorities and their attitude towards ethnic aspirations in other republics. That's not clear to me, as a matter of fact. Could you be -- could you explain it for me. Did you want to express, for example, that constructing 700 mosques would find no opposition whatsoever, and therefore it indicated how the -- how liberal the government was towards religion, or what -- what exactly do you mean by the words you -- in your answer?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant tolerance. I meant the tolerant climate which reigned in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was the same tolerance effective in respect of other religions?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I have to say that after 1945, the majority of the population of the SFRY, both under the Communist rule, were atheist by and large, and in the Orthodox church -- and the Orthodox church and the Muslims were not particularly happy to hear that you were a communist and you went to -- you attended service in the church, and therefore, since everybody had one political party and a large part of the population were members of that one party, religion was not a topical subject in that country.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to ask you a few questions about your comments on the Markale incident. And I'm referring to the incident you describe at -- in your report in great detail, that is, the 5th of February, 1994. You said that the attention was drawn -- the attention of the public was drawn to some facts, one of them being that 80 per cent of the wounds inflicted by explosion were on the lower extremities of the bodies. What is the source for this fact?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The source is my conversation with Colonel Demurenko, who at a later stage assessed Markale II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So it is on the basis of Mr. Demurenko that you accept or at least that you did write down in your report that 80 per cent of the wounds inflicted were of the lower extremities of the bodies. Was Mr. Demurenko present at the market when the incident took place?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Demurenko was not present at the time of the first incident in Markale in 1994. He was present only at the time of Markale II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What would be the source of his information as to the injuries for 80 per cent inflicted on the lower parts of the body?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you will be in a position to ask Colonel Demurenko about it. But from what I could gather, he juxtaposed the incidents in 1995 and 1994, because he was interested in the subject and it is quite possible that he had some supplementary information. I have the recording of my conversation with him. And if I remember, it was enclosed with my expert opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I don't doubt that Mr. Demurenko told you. But I was just wondering what the actual source of this information was. Could I -- you also mention that there were testimonies that a little while before the explosion bodies of just deceased persons were brought to the marketplace. What are these testimonies? Are they published, or did you gather this also from your conversation with Mr. Demurenko?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my footnotes I make reference to the file which was compiled by the Ministry of Information of Serbia, and it is entitled "Pijaca Markale file, Markale market file."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have not looked that up. I hope you'll understand that the Chamber has not been able to verify all the sources you used, and that's the reason I'm asking you. Are names mentioned in this file or the names of the witnesses who testified and where, under what circumstances they testified?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, I think that we have this document in our centre. And if you don't have it here, we can send it to you, the document I mean. But I couldn't really tell you off the cuff. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then my next question is about -- you have -- I read part of your report where it says, "According to the recollections of Lord Owen in Zagreb, one of the UNPROFOR officers, a ballistic expert by specialisation, was studying the possible trajectories of the shells and concluded that the firing point was located along the positions of the Muslim army." And then you go on literally quoting the publication of Lord Owen. The first sentence, which is not a literal quote, do you have the original text of what you are paraphrasing here? I'll tell you why I'm asking: Because it says that "The firing point was located along the positions of the Muslim army." That suggests that an exact firing point was not located. And therefore, I'm quite interested to know what exactly were the conclusions according to Lord Owen. Do you have the literal part of this book, especially on this subject?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was asked by our people to copy all the quotations that I intended to use here. And as likely as not one can find it photocopied in the footnotes, I gather, and we can look it up. This is not in the Serb version of my text -- I mean the footnotes. But -- but being a scientist, being a researcher, I can tell you that I didn't put things in inverted commas, only when I would use -- I would quote only a word or two from some text. That is why I didn't put inverted commas. But this sentence was taken from David Owen's book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The reason why I'm asking you is that although this Chamber has seen reports, ballistic reports on the incident, it is not my recollection that it was any of these reports that would say that the firing point was located along the positions of the Muslim army. Therefore, I'm just wondering whether there would be a report unknown to this Chamber that would contain such a conclusion. But you say you haven't got the book with you. Perhaps we could check in the original of the book. The problem is the book was on loan in the library, so I can't do it right away. Then my next question would be -- and I'm specifically interested to know whether there are any reports unknown to this Chamber. You refer to -- and you are quoting Mr. Akashi in an interview -- "the existence of a secret report was never --"

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can answer that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you said -- well, you don't know yet what my question is about that secret report. And you say, "And that many journalists disposed with the copies of its text." Did you ever see the text of this report? Because I'm very much interested to know whether it's in the report unknown to us or whether this is a report which is known to this Chamber. Did you ever see the text of that report?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't have it in my hands, and I didn't want to quote journalists. However, the atmosphere that I observed in Zagreb at the time when possible versions of the Markale case were being discussed and what Yasushi Akashi had to say about it tells me that such a document is in existence, and I believe that the Tribunal should have that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps we have the document. But if you have not seen the text, it's difficult for us to compare the documents we have available and those documents which you say that they were in the hands of journalists. My --

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not saying -- I'm not saying that the journalists had it. They were trying to quote him. But Yasushi Akashi spoke about its existence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. But at least there's no possibility for us to verify if we haven't got the text of the report you are referring to in the words of Mr. Akashi. Then --

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it is very good that we agreed that there was a document which was missing in the Tribunal, and I believe it will be -- you will be able to locate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't think that we agreed on anything at all. The only thing I said is that in order to establish whether the report you're referring to is a report which is not available to the Tribunal is to compare the two documents. And since we've only the documents available to us and not the potential missing document, we did not agree on anything. It has still to be established. Then you told us about the report of the Secretary-General of the 19th of May, 1992, which came on the desk of the members of the Security Council only after a resolution had been adopted. You were confronted with the text of it and some questions were put to you as far as the preparation of this report is concerned. And did I understand your testimony correctly where it -- that the final version of that report was not available when the members of the Security Council were voting on the resolution but that a draft report was available, because you mentioned an earlier draft?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think you understood me correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When confronted with a certain line and asked whether this would not indicate that the report was not prepared before the resolution was adopted, you told us that this might be a version different from a draft. I took that to be a previous version. But please explain what you then meant.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may interrupt. I beg your pardon. The date of the report is 30th May 1992, not 19th May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think I said 1992. But at least I mentioned -- at least I meant to say the 30th of May. But yes, could you please explain then what you meant while talking about a draft or an earlier version of that report.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was yesterday when we started talking about the document of the 30th of May, 1992. It was then that I asked you to allow me to speak out, because I wanted to look at the computer which I have here with me and I wanted to look up the Russian version of the Secretary-General's report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I -- and in relation to what I had already looked up at home, and I even printed out the seventeenth item of the report and have it with me, because it will prove to us fully today that I was absolutely right when I said that this report had been prepared for the session of the Security Council but had not found its way to the desk. But the text of this item 17 is very important for us now, and it reads like this: "Today's resolution of the Security Council to impose sanctions on Yugoslavia creates a new situation. It is not clear yet what will be the effect of this on issues considered in this report." So the word "today" or "today's" tells us that the report was to have been put on the desks of the members of the Security Council of the 30th of May, yet it appeared -- it emerged only a few days later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The last part of your answer you say it "have been put on the desks on the 30th of May and it emerged only a few days later." How exactly did you establish that it appeared a few days later? I mean --

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This fact is common knowledge. Now, yesterday I explained that on the 30th this report was not on the desks, that the voting took place -- that they voted without having discussed before that the report of the Secretary-General. All this information we received in the parliament of the Russian federation in early June, at the time when this issue was on the agenda.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I've got no difficulties to accept that if the report refers to something that happened on that same day that it could not be -- have been written prior to that day. Nevertheless, I still do not understand what supports -- what is the basis for your assumption that it was -- it emerged only a couple of days later. You say that is common knowledge. Is that the basis of this fact you establish?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you need corroboration of what I'm saying, that this report was not on the desks at the time of the vote on sanctions against Yugoslavia, then I suppose one has to look at the protocols, at the records of the Security Council. I came by this information from the documents that were available in our parliament and the statement made by our representative in the Security Council.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. I nevertheless would like to take you back to your testimony of yesterday. One of your answers was, "Based on the fact that the report itself appeared later, it is quite possible that it was written up later on. When we analysed this at our parliament session, this paragraph was missing. It wasn't there. We had it in a different draft." I have some problems in reconciling your answer of today where you quoted in Russian exactly the same paragraph as read out yesterday to you. Yesterday you said that you had not the same paragraph in the report you studied, and today you confirm to me that it was exactly this paragraph 17 that is of such importance.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not saying that it is irrelevant or non-important. Simply yesterday I could not derive from English why this paragraph did not lead me to think about this and to raise this issue in those days, in 1992. That is why I could not simply reconstruct this in my memory. I simply needed to have a look at the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was just a presupposition which I was speaking about. I checked the document, and today we dotted all the I's.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. I have some more questions for you, but I'd prefer first to have a break. But it will not take much time after the break. We'll adjourn until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Usher, could you please. Professor Guskova, I have the following question for you: In your report you write about the suspicions in respect of the explosion in a bread queue on Vase Miskina Street. Do you know what happened? I mean, apart from it seems you suggest that the BiH forces or at least not the Serb forces were responsible for that explosion, and you give some reasons for suspicion. Do you have any knowledge on what actually happened? I mean, apart from -- I do understand your doubts, but could you bring us any further?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not have any additional information at my disposal with regard to what happened in Vase Miskina Street.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then my next question again goes to your reflection of what Lord Owen writes in his book. You say that a ballistic expert was studying the possible trajectories of the shells and concluded that the firing point was located along the positions of the Muslim army. Did he -- how firm was his conclusion and on what was it based, according to Lord Owen?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I believe that this question should be referred to Lord Owen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. You are writing -- you're reflecting the book of Lord Owen, so therefore I think it would be perfectly right to put the question to you, since you paraphrased the book of Lord Owen. Does Lord Owen give any specification as to whether this was a probability or whether this was a firm conclusion or whether this was a possibility or -- and on what was it based?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lord Owen writes specifically that according to his recollections, in Zagreb there was a ballistics expert who expressed his opinions with regard to Markale I and he mentions him, although does not name him. However, I believe that here another thing is rather important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But could you please concentrate on my question and answer my question. I'm not asking you whether Lord Owen refers to a ballistic expert. I'll be glad to accept that. But what does Lord Owen exactly write about the conclusion of this expert?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I understand, he takes him as a fact for information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not asking whether he takes him -- no, please listen to my question. In what terms he describes the -- what you present as a conclusion and on the basis of what?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry to say that I do not quite get your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you say that Lord Owen writes that a ballistic expert was studying the possible trajectories of the shells and - and now comes the most relevant part - and concluded that the firing point was located along the positions of the Muslim army. Would that mean that Lord Owen presents this conclusion as that the shell was fired from a position along the positions of the Muslim army?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Didn't Lord Owen write that this expert thought it more probable that the shell was fired from within a distance of 2.000 metres rather than from a distance between 2 and 3 thousand metres?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Since further on he describes why this information was kept secret from everybody else, from all the other peacekeeping forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just asking you about what according to Lord Owen's book the conclusion of the expert was. And I asked you whether it is not true that the expert expressed himself in probabilities where he thought under 2.000 metres was more probable than between 2 and 3 thousand metres distance.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would answer negatively to your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it was a conclusion that the shell was fired from along the positions of the Muslim army.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am convinced of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. My next question would be -- yes. My last question to you is: You have explained at several -- in several parts of your report that the Serbs would not opposed -- be opposed against being in a federation -- a Bosnian-Herzegovinian federation if they would have their own specific entity that would allow them later to seek to join with the Republic of Serbia and that the Muslims were very much opposed to this and they wanted to be independent. I've been wondering whether my understanding would be correct that if the Bosnian Serbs would remain within a federation with the Muslims and the Croats, that they would be a approximately 30 to 35 per cent minority of the population, although holding approximately 50 per cent of the land, and would therefore be in an unfavourable position, whereas if they would join with the Republic of Serbia that they would have a stronger position on the territory. Is that a correct understanding of why the other parties were very much in favour of an independent Bosnia-Herzegovina, whereas the Bosnian Serbs would rather not be cut off from other Serbs outside Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have a correct understanding of this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much then for your -- for your answers. Is there any need to put further questions to the witness? Yes. Perhaps we now can first give the -- give you the opportunity to say what you wanted to say. But there might be some additional questions by the -- by the parties after that. Yes, please proceed. Tell us what you wanted to tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. I had a question to you. Yesterday for quite a while we were discussing one document which interprets the session of skupstina or element of Republika Srpska of the 12th of May. And we did not talk about the document itself, the document of skupstina. I deem that the Tribunal does not have this document at its disposal and would like to say that in Moscow, in our centre we have this document and we could provide it to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As far as -- you mean the strategic objectives, the six ones in the original document? Is that -- yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think we have that available in the Tribunal. So that -- as far as I remember, it was also one of the annexes to one of the expert reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we have it available. It's already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry you had to remain in uncertainty for such a long time, but -- Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Further examination by Mr. Piletta-Zanin:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, madam. You spoke to us about this residual section in the census, the section that one refers to as Yugoslavs. Many questions were put to you about this. My question is as follows: Within the three category that is we are interested in - the Croats, the Muslims, and the Serbs - was there one category which in terms of nature and history was more inclined to declare themselves as being Yugoslavs for intrinsic reasons? I am not talking about figures at the moment. I'm talking about internal characteristics.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is exactly what I wanted to explain when I was asked about the notion of Yugoslavs. The whole crisis itself in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, starting from 1991, demonstrates that from all the peoples populating the former Yugoslavia only Serbs were attempting to maintain the Federation. All the others were striving to exit the Federation and create states of their own. That is why sociological surveys and studies confirm our line of thinking that the idea of Yugoslavism to a greater extent was present among the Serbian and Montenegrin population and a little bit, to a lower extent, among the Montenegrin people, I would say --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Macedonian people. Correction by interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, witness. And the formulation Muslim Yugoslav at the time, would there have been an antagonism? Would there have been a contradiction between these two terms in the way that Croat and Yugoslav, these two term, could be contradictory? Have you understood my question?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understood the question in general. However, I would like to state that among the Muslims there were also Yugoslavs, those who would register themselves as Yugoslavs. This has to deal with their origins which they remembered as Serbian or Croatian. However, this number was very low as compared to the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, in response to one of the questions put to you, by Judge El Mahdi, I think, you said that the census on 1991 - nine-one - wasn't sufficiently official or wasn't sufficiently credible, I think. I can't remember what you said exactly, but I think that that was the idea. What did you mean with regard that this subject and in comparison to the other two censuses that we are aware of, 1971 and 1981?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The matter is that the census of 1991, the results of that census should have appeared a little bit later after they were drawn and at that very moment the fire of the conflicts escalated in the territory of the former Yugoslavia. That is why any official data confirmed by signature at the level of the state is not available. However, we could see that published in many magazines, but at the same time it is considered that there might have been some adjustments made in other republics pursuant to the altering situation. That is why the United Nations organisation, in its consideration of inter-ethnical issues, would always refer to the census of 1991 -- 1981.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. When you say this, can you be more specific and can you tell us about the scientific reliability of the document of 1991, which was elaborated in December 1993.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which document are you referring to? I didn't quite get that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm referring to the same document, the census of 1991. And we know that it was elaborated in December 1993. My question concerns the scientific reliability, the reliability of this document if one is to base scientific research on it.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the documents of the census which emerged during the periods starting from 1991 and further on should be seriously scrutinised and checked from the scientific point of view. Since I know from our own experience on the example of Croatia and the Republic of Srpska Krajina and Zagreb, lists would be published on the statistical data about the population, which were totally different and did not match, in that very period from 1991 to 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. When you say that there were discrepancies, can you tell us whether this was accidental, there were certain shortcomings in certain documents, errors, or was this organised in a voluntary manner, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I am absolutely convinced that the alteration of data was taking place in accordance with the political situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, I would now like to move on to the issue of the double blockade. Judge El Mahdi asked you a certain number of questions about this double blockade, and he wanted to know whether you agreed with what Mr. Owen had declared. I'd like you to focus on my question with regard to what Lord Owen said. What do you know about the statement according to which sniper fire or the shelling of civilians was allegedly organised by the Serbian forces? What do you know about this?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you asking about the origins or causes for this, or are you asking what Lord Owen thought about this?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. I am asking you a question to an extent that you answered in affirmative terms the question put to you by Judge El Mahdi. I want to know what you personally know about an alleged campaign of shelling and of sniper fire which was directed against civilians by the Serbian forces. This is my question. If you don't know anything about it, just tell us.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object. This doesn't arise from the questions put by Judge El Mahdi. In fact, the question was with regard -- as to whether the witness accepted the statement of Lord Owen, the statement attributable to him where he claims -- speaks about the two blockades.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apart from whether it arises from -- I think the -- having consulted also with Judge El Mahdi, that the witness has Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 19542 to 19554. answered the questions as to what her own knowledge is and what was the source of what she wrote about in her report. Therefore, the objection is sustained. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'll move on to another subject.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It concerns the well-known secret report in which the conclusions of this report -- in which conclusions were reached, and you mentioned about it with regard to Mr. Owen. And I'm referring to the Markale incident. You were questioned by Judge Orie earlier on about what Lord Owen wrote in his book with regard to the origin of fire, if there was such an origin, in the case of this incident. My question is as follows: Was there and can you be specific about this if it is the case -- were there any other elements that would have enabled you to support this conclusion that was reached in the report or to support the different conclusions -- or to support different conclusions than we spoke about earlier on? I'm talking about the substance, not about the form of what Mr. Owen said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before the witness could answer this question, should it not be first be established what according to Lord Owen the conclusions of the report were?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Gladly. Gladly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were asked -- you asked what Mr. Owen said, according to this witness, with regard to the origin of fire. To be more precise, this is the issue that concerns -- the issue of alongside the mines [as interpreted]. Contrary to other factors, for example, 2 or 3 thousand metres. What I want to know is whether this witness was aware of any other elements that might support the first deduction that you summarised in your report. Could you answer that question.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to draw the attention of the report to the Secretary-General of the United Nations organisation of the 15th of November, 1999. I have it in my computer, and I could show it to you if you don't have it at your disposal. In paragraph 119, it is stipulated that the first studies of the United Nations organisation of the crater of the explosion demonstrated that the bomb had been launched from the Bosnian side from the combat lines or possibly detonated on the spot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the transcript, Mr. President, in line 37 I was talking "alongside lines," not "mines".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That was clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I just wanted to make it clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My last question: You were asked about a high number or the increasing number of mosques at a certain period of time. My question is as follows: Could one establish certain parallism [as interpreted] between this, say, religious activity, that is, the increase in the number of houses of worship and the political situation, according to your experience? On the Muslim side, obviously.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I didn't really understand your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will rephrase it and cut it shorter. Could one draw a parallel between what I call the religious activism and the political attitude of the Muslims during that period of time? Could one draw some conclusions that there -- that these two were developing in parallel?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one could do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just to understand your question better. Do you refer to the construction of a high number of mosques? Is that what you call religious activism, Mr. Piletta-Zanin? Just to clarify the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have said that quite clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You said that. But is -- you were referring to the construction of mosques.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, quite so, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's clear. And I take it that you understood the question in that sense?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any further questions from the ...?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I need to consult. I need to consult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one more question, but it will be Mrs. Pilipovic who will ask it, because it will be shorter then.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, with your leave, a clarification, a question for Mrs. Guskova. She said that she was quoting Lord Owen with regard to the blockade, so my question is whether Madam Professor could tell us if she knows what a blockade is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I answer that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I understand the question, it is an extension of a question that I was already asked before, whether I went along with Mr. Owen's definition or phrasing. I think that that is not an accurate phrasing. There was no full complete external blockade that is a circle around Sarajevo. In one of the reports of the Secretary-General - and it is the same report that I mentioned a while ago - in item 2, in 176, the Secretary-General, as early as 1990, says that there was a road used for army transports across Igman and Bjelasnica and which led directly into the heart of the city. Moreover, there was a tunnel under the airport, and everybody knows about that. There were also humanitarian relief convoys. And all this tells us that -- testifies that the term "blockade" is rather -- should be understood in rather conditional terms.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is there any need for further questions? Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May the witness be shown the 1991 census. Perhaps my copy can be shown to her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When we talk again about the 1991 census, Ms. Mahindaratne, may I remind you that the issue has been raised by you in order to ask questions about a certain part of the report, whereas the witness has testified that when she was talking about a majority of Serbs that this was only the territory controlled by the Bosnian Serb army, not necessarily the full territory of these municipalities, and that it was the situation at 1993 or the second part of 1992. And I don't know whether the parties do agree on the fact that at least some movement of population has taken place at the beginning of the conflict. So I'm not disallowing you to go into the 1991 census again, but please keep in mind the testimony of the witness on how she used these figures concerning the population, in what areas exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I just need to verify with regard to her position that this is not an official census and the fact that it's not the final statistics. I just merely needed to get that fact out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps I have taken too much of the time, but ... Further cross-examination by Ms. Mahindaratne:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, would you please read out the name of the body - it is on the cover page of the census - the body which has published this census.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The results of this census -- of this census were published by the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the State Republic Statistics Administration. But this information came out in 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just interrupt you. Would you mind to have the document on the ELMO and read it from there so that we also can see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps in the interest of time, madam, I will -- would you agree with me that the body that has published in document is the state office for statistics of Bosnia and Herzegovina? That's what the -- what it reads on the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't agree with you because the 1991 census took place whilst SFRY was still in one piece. And I've already explained the situation in this regard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please read the name of the body which is printed on the top of the first page, the cover page. That's all I'm asking you to do, madam. Just read from the cover page the name of the body which has published this census. It is at the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can repeat: I've already read it. The Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina State Statistics administration of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We are sorry. There were several speakers speaking at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't mind this. But to make the witness to read and reread and then reread once again the witness one and the same thing, I don't think this is particularly productive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's not a -- such disastrous that it would need an intervention. There seems to be some -- some misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. I will go on to my next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please turn to the next page, madam, page 2. Can you read out what it says there. Does it indicate that it is the final statistics? Is the word "final statistics" or "final data" mentioned there?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see a seal there and a signature?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who has signed that document, the position of the person who has signed.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hasan Zoljic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was his position?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, presumably the director of the statistics administration or institute.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise that seal on the document?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So would you agree that it is an official document giving out final statistics?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I disagree with that statement. Why? Because the 1991 census took place whilst the Federation still existed, and all the official data were verified by the central statistics administration in Belgrade, which was the state institution of the Federation as a whole. And since, all the data after that, were also published at the republican level at the time when the political situation was not stable, leads me to believe that this data, these figures, are the figures of the republics, rather than the figures provided by the Federation or arrived at by federal bodies as had been -- as was to be the case in the census of 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Sorry, Ms. Mahindaratne. As we are talking about the statement that we have on the ELMO and we don't have the translation, could you ask the witness or the interpreters to translate the statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, could you read out the statement on page 2 in full.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you to do it slowly because we know that while reading, speed goes up usually.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 2: "Foreword, preface. This is one in a series of bulletins published by the state statistics administration of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina relative to the census of the population, household, residential units, and farms in 1991. The bulletin encompasses the final results, the final data on the ethnicity of the population per settlement." And then "Sarajevo, December 1993, director Hasan Zoljic."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, madam. In reference to a question about the Markale incident --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is not directly related to a question from the Bench but following from a response given by the witness to a question from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may formulate the question. We'll then decide whether the witness can answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You referred to a report of the Secretary-General of 15th of November, 1999 where you claim the report refers to the Markale shell being fired from the, to use your own words, "the BH side." My question to you is: Did I understand you well? Is that date correct, 15th November 1999?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is this report? Do you know the number of the report? Generally the Secretary-General's report bears a particular number. Could you give out the number of that report.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I switch on my computer, and then I'll -- and I'll give you the exact number. It deals with the response to resolution 53/35.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you may consult your computer if you stored your data in that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here it is. The number of the document, A54/549. If you want me to, I can show you the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see that you have a laptop showing the document. I see that you have a copy. What --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is an official UN document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I wonder whether we could peruse this document. Perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps we could do another thing. If we would have an early break, we perhaps could have it printed and then it's available in printed form that comes from our library or from the laptop of Professor Guskova. Yes. Ms. Pilipovic, we might even have a CD-ROM copy. Yes. So the number is available now to the Prosecution. Did you have any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you read the relevant portion of that report where it states that the explosion, and to use your word, that it had either originated from the Bosnian side or it was due to an impact on the spot? And that is as I recall the words used by you. Could you read that particular portion which due to you assert your position.

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I read out to you was the quotation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. In fact you referred to the paragraph -- you say paragraph 119. It is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If -- if we want to pay attention to the specific text of this document, should it then not be printed out during the break and that we -- because that's an easier way of dealing with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you have any other questions on any other subjects?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes. Just one more, Mr. President. I'll move on and then come back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would move to that and then perhaps we'll have an early break and then look at the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, you stated that those who claim to be Yugoslavian were mostly of Serbian origin. Isn't it the case that the Yugoslav census were all based on self-declaration and not on an analysis of ancestry, religion, or name? Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: ELENA GUSKOVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you referred to surveys -- you referred to sociological and ideological surveys which confirmed this fact. Could you refer to such a survey conducted by a particular body that you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just ask you. It's not my recollection that the witness referred to ideological surveys but, rather, statistical -- statistical analysis. Or am I wrong?
